name: McLaren Vale
summary: Mediterranean-climate region south of Adelaide between the Mount Lofty Ranges and Gulf St Vincent, home to some of Australia's oldest Grenache and Shiraz vines and a leader in sustainable and alternative-variety viticulture.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, moderated by sea breezes from the gulf; dry summers and winter rainfall.
soils: Exceptionally varied geology, from ancient Cambrian schist and quartzite to sand over clay, terra rossa, ironstone and limestone; mapped as 19 distinct districts.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Mourvèdre, plus a growing range of Mediterranean grapes such as Fiano, Vermentino, Tempranillo and Nero d'Avola.

name: South Australia
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across several South Australian regions. The state makes around half of Australia's wine.
climate: Ranges from hot inland irrigated areas to cool, elevated and maritime regions in the Adelaide Hills and Limestone Coast.
soils: Diverse: red-brown earths, terra rossa over limestone, sandy loams and ironstone; phylloxera-free, so many vineyards are on their own roots.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Barossa Valley
summary: Australia's best-known wine region, settled by Silesian Lutherans in the 1840s, with some of the world's oldest continuously producing Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre vines.
climate: Warm and dry continental, with hot summer days and cool nights; low rainfall makes old dry-grown vines prized.
soils: Varied red-brown earths, sandy loams and grey-brown clays over limestone and ironstone; deep sand in the north-west.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Grenache, Mourvèdre (Mataro), Cabernet Sauvignon, Semillon.
blends: GSM, Shiraz–Cabernet; fortified Tawny and Apera traditions.

name: Adelaide Hills
summary: Elevated, cool region in the Mount Lofty Ranges just east of Adelaide; South Australia's go-to source for crisp whites, sparkling base and elegant reds.
climate: Cool to moderate, with altitude (400–700 m) driving long ripening, cool nights and higher rainfall than the plains.
soils: Sandy loams and clay over weathered schist, sandstone and ironstone.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Shiraz, Grüner Veltliner, Gamay.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling (Chardonnay–Pinot Noir); cool-climate Shiraz often co-fermented with Viognier.

name: Clare Valley
summary: A series of narrow north–south valleys north of Adelaide, famous for bone-dry, lime-scented Riesling that ages for decades, especially from the Watervale and Polish Hill sub-regions.
climate: Continental with warm days and markedly cool nights, plus elevation (300–500 m) that preserves acidity.
soils: Terra rossa over limestone (Watervale) and slate and shale (Polish Hill), with red-brown loams elsewhere.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Malbec.
blends: Cabernet–Malbec is a regional speciality; also Shiraz–Cabernet.

name: Langhorne Creek
summary: Flat, fertile region on the Bremer and Angas river floodplains near Lake Alexandrina, a key supplier of soft, generous reds to many South Australian blends.
climate: Moderate maritime, cooled by the 'Lake Doctor' breeze off Lake Alexandrina.
soils: Deep alluvial sandy and clay loams, historically flood-irrigated by winter floods.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Merlot, Montepulciano.
blends: Cabernet–Shiraz and Cabernet–Malbec blends; components for multi-regional labels.

name: Coonawarra
summary: A narrow 27 km cigar-shaped strip on the Limestone Coast, renowned for structured, mint- and cassis-tinged Cabernet Sauvignon grown on its famous red soil.
climate: Cool maritime, influenced by Southern Ocean winds; long, even ripening with frost risk in spring.
soils: Terra rossa: a thin band of red, iron-rich clay loam over limestone and a high water table.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling.

name: Yarra Valley
summary: Victoria's first wine region, just north-east of Melbourne, producing elegant, finely structured Chardonnay and Pinot Noir and a strong sparkling tradition.
climate: Cool, with marked variation from the warmer valley floor to the cold, higher Upper Yarra.
soils: Grey sandy clay loams over sandstone on the valley floor; deep red volcanic soils in the Upper Yarra.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Nebbiolo.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling; Bordeaux-style Cabernet blends; Shiraz–Viognier.

name: Riverland
summary: South Australia's largest-volume region along the Murray River, the engine room of affordable Australian wine and an increasingly interesting source of alternative varieties.
climate: Hot, dry continental with high sunshine; relies on Murray River irrigation.
soils: Red sandy loams and calcareous sands over limestone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot, plus Fiano, Montepulciano, Nero d'Avola and Vermentino.
blends: Value red and white blends; components for South Eastern Australia labels.

name: Eden Valley
summary: The elevated, rugged eastern neighbour of the Barossa (part of the Barossa zone), producing taut, floral Riesling and finely spiced Shiraz, including some of Australia's most famous single vineyards.
climate: Cool for South Australia thanks to altitude (380–550 m); later ripening than the Barossa floor.
soils: Thin, rocky, acidic soils of weathered schist, quartz and ironstone.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Viognier.
blends: Mostly varietal wines; Eden Valley fruit is often blended into Barossa Shiraz.

name: Margaret River
summary: Western Australia's flagship region on a peninsula between two oceans, producing a large share of Australia's premium Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
climate: Maritime Mediterranean, the most marine-influenced in Australia; warm, dry summers and mild winters.
soils: Gravelly and sandy loams over granite and gneiss; ironstone gravels prized for Cabernet.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Merlot, Shiraz.

name: Southern Fleurieu
summary: Small, cool region at the southern tip of the Fleurieu Peninsula, between McLaren Vale and Cape Jervis, best known for brisk whites and medium-bodied reds.
climate: Cool maritime, exposed to Southern Ocean and gulf winds.
soils: Sandy loams and podzolic soils over ironstone and weathered schist.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Victoria
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across Victorian regions. Victoria has more wine regions than any other state, from the cool south coast to the warm north-east.
climate: From cool maritime (Mornington, Geelong) and alpine (Macedon) to warm inland (Rutherglen, Murray Darling).
soils: Very varied: volcanic basalts, granite-derived sands, ancient sedimentary and alluvial soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Riesling, Muscat.
blends: Cross-regional Shiraz and sparkling; Rutherglen Muscat and Topaque fortifieds.

name: Tasmania
summary: Australia's coolest wine state, island-wide a single GI, now the country's benchmark for sparkling wine and a fast-rising source of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling.
climate: Cool maritime, with long, mild growing seasons and high natural acidity.
soils: Dolerite- and basalt-derived soils, sandstone, mudstone and river gravels, varying by valley (Tamar, Coal River, Derwent, Huon).
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

name: Grampians
summary: Western Victorian region at the foot of the Grampians ranges, centred on Great Western, with a long history of spicy, peppery cool-climate Shiraz and sparkling Shiraz.
climate: Cool to moderate continental, with significant altitude and diurnal range.
soils: Grey-brown sandy loams over clay, and weathered sandstone and granite.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Meunier.

name: Great Western
summary: Historic sub-region of the Grampians, home to Seppelt and Best's since the 1860s and some of Victoria's oldest Shiraz vines; birthplace of Australian sparkling Shiraz.
climate: Cool continental with low rainfall; frost and drought are the main risks.
soils: Grey-brown loamy sands over clay and decomposed granite.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Pinot Meunier, Chardonnay.
blends: Sparkling Shiraz; field-blend plantings in old nurseries.

name: Geelong
summary: Cool maritime region on Port Phillip Bay's western side, including the Bellarine Peninsula and Moorabool Valley, known for intense, mineral Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Shiraz.
climate: Cool, dry and windy maritime, with low rainfall and small yields.
soils: Black cracking volcanic clays over limestone (Moorabool) and sandy loams on the Bellarine.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.

name: Murray Darling
summary: Large, irrigated region straddling the Murray River between Victoria and New South Wales, around Mildura; a major source of everyday Australian wine.
climate: Hot, sunny and dry continental; dependent on river irrigation.
soils: Red-brown sandy loams and calcareous sands (Mallee soils).
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, plus alternative grapes such as Fiano, Nero d'Avola and Lagrein.
blends: Value blends and components for South Eastern Australia labels.

name: New South Wales
summary: State-level designation for wines blended across New South Wales regions, from the historic Hunter Valley to the high country of Orange and the irrigated Riverina.
climate: Humid subtropical (Hunter), cool elevated (Orange, Tumbarumba), hot inland (Riverina).
soils: Varied: alluvial loams, volcanic basalt, and red-brown earths.
typical_varietals: Semillon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Cross-regional reds; Riverina botrytis Semillon dessert wines.

name: Heathcote
summary: Central Victorian region along the Mount Camel Range, famous for deep, plush yet savoury Shiraz grown on ancient red Cambrian soil.
climate: Warm continental, moderated by the range's altitude and cooling southerly winds.
soils: Deep red Cambrian greenstone soil (weathered volcanic rock over 500 million years old).
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Nebbiolo, Tempranillo, Sangiovese.

name: Wrattonbully
summary: Limestone Coast region just north of Coonawarra, planted mostly since the 1990s, producing well-structured Cabernet, Shiraz and Merlot.
climate: Cool to moderate maritime with good air drainage on gentle slopes, reducing frost risk.
soils: Terra rossa and sandy loams over limestone, similar to Coonawarra.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Merlot, Tempranillo, Chardonnay.
blends: Cabernet–Merlot; often blended with Coonawarra fruit.

name: Great Southern
summary: Western Australia's largest and coolest region, with five sub-regions (Albany, Denmark, Frankland River, Mount Barker, Porongurup); known for intense Riesling and peppery Shiraz.
climate: Cool maritime near the coast and more continental inland, with long, slow ripening.
soils: Lateritic gravelly loams and sandy soils over ancient granite.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

name: Padthaway
summary: Limestone Coast region north of Coonawarra, established in the 1960s, supplying quality Chardonnay and Shiraz to many large producers.
climate: Moderate maritime, slightly warmer than Coonawarra.
soils: Terra rossa and brown sandy loams over limestone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

name: Alpine Valleys
summary: North-east Victorian region of river valleys (Ovens, Kiewa, Buffalo, Buckland) beneath the Victorian Alps, with a strong Italian-variety tradition.
climate: Cool to warm depending on altitude, with cold nights and high rainfall.
soils: Alluvial and granitic soils on valley floors, red loams on slopes.
typical_varietals: Prosecco (Glera), Tempranillo, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay.

name: Pyrenees
summary: Central Victorian region around Avoca and Moonambel, known for robust, minty Shiraz and Cabernet and some sparkling.
climate: Moderate continental with cool nights from altitude.
soils: Grey-brown loams and sandy soils over clay, with quartz gravels.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: King Valley
summary: North-east Victorian valley settled by Italian families, the Australian home of Prosecco and other Italian varieties.
climate: Ranges from warm on the valley floor to cool at Whitlands (up to 800 m).
soils: Red and grey loams, alluvial soils on the valley floor.
typical_varietals: Prosecco (Glera), Pinot Grigio, Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Barbera, Riesling.

name: Macedon Ranges
summary: Mainland Australia's coolest wine region, north-west of Melbourne, producing taut sparkling wine, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
climate: Very cool and windy continental, with altitude up to 800 m; ripening can be marginal.
soils: Granite-derived sandy soils and volcanic basalt loams.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Shiraz.

name: Goulburn Valley
summary: Central Victorian region along the Goulburn River, including the Nagambie Lakes sub-region, home to Tahbilk's 1860 Shiraz and the world's largest Marsanne plantings.
climate: Warm continental, moderated by the river and lakes around Nagambie.
soils: Red sandy loams with high iron content and alluvial river soils.
typical_varietals: Marsanne, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Roussanne, Viognier.

name: Hunter Valley
summary: Australia's oldest continuously operating wine region, north of Sydney, famous for low-alcohol, long-lived Semillon and medium-bodied, earthy Shiraz.
climate: Warm, humid subtropical, with summer rain and cloud cover during vintage.
soils: Sandy alluvial flats (best for Semillon) and red volcanic and clay loams on slopes (Shiraz).
typical_varietals: Semillon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Verdelho.
blends: Mostly varietal; historic 'Hunter Burgundy' Shiraz–Pinot styles.

name: Mudgee
summary: Elevated region on the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range in New South Wales, known for rich reds and Chardonnay.
climate: Warm continental with altitude (450–1,100 m) and cold nights.
soils: Sandy loams over clay, with some volcanic soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Barbera.

name: Orange
summary: High-altitude New South Wales region on the slopes of the extinct volcano Mount Canobolas, defined by a minimum altitude of 600 m.
climate: Cool continental from altitude; frost and snow are possible.
soils: Red-brown basalt-derived volcanic soils and limestone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Canberra District
summary: Cool region surrounding the national capital, best known for Shiraz co-fermented with Viognier and for Riesling.
climate: Cool continental with cold winters and hot, dry summer days.
soils: Shallow granitic and shale soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

name: Rutherglen
summary: North-east Victorian region famous for luscious fortified Muscat and Topaque (Muscadelle), aged for decades in old barrels.
climate: Hot continental, with long, dry autumns ideal for raisining fruit.
soils: Red loams and sandy alluvial soils.
typical_varietals: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge, Muscadelle (Topaque), Durif, Shiraz.
blends: Fortified Muscat and Topaque, graded Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare.

name: Mornington Peninsula
summary: Maritime peninsula south of Melbourne surrounded by water on three sides, producing elegant Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.
climate: Cool maritime, moderated by Port Phillip and Western Port bays.
soils: Red volcanic soils, brown duplex soils and sandy loams.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Shiraz.

name: Beechworth
summary: Small, elevated north-east Victorian region with a cult following for complex Chardonnay and savoury Shiraz.
climate: Cool to moderate continental with altitude.
soils: Granite-derived gravels and some ancient shale and sandstone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Nebbiolo, Sangiovese.

name: Frankland River
summary: The most northerly and inland sub-region of Great Southern, noted for perfumed Riesling and structured Shiraz and Cabernet.
climate: Cool continental, dry and with a large diurnal range.
soils: Gravelly lateritic loams over granite and gneiss.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec.

name: Kangaroo Island
summary: South Australia's island region off the Fleurieu Peninsula, with a small number of producers making maritime-influenced reds and whites.
climate: Cool maritime, with constant ocean breezes.
soils: Sandy loams over ironstone and limestone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.

name: Aconcagua
summary: Region north of Santiago named after the Americas' highest peak, including the cool coastal Casablanca and San Antonio valleys and the warmer inland Aconcagua Valley.
climate: Warm inland, cooled by the Andes at night; coastal sub-regions are cool from the Humboldt Current.
soils: Alluvial and colluvial gravels inland; granite and clay on the coast.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carmenère, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir (coastal).

name: Central Valley
summary: Chile's heartland of wine production between the Andes and the Coastal Range, including the Maipo, Rapel (Colchagua, Cachapoal), Curicó and Maule valleys.
climate: Warm Mediterranean with dry summers and a large diurnal range from Andes breezes.
soils: Alluvial gravels and loams, with granite in the Coastal Range.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, País, Carignan.
blends: Cabernet–Carmenère; old-vine Carignan blends (VIGNO) in Maule.

name: Shandong
summary: Coastal province on the Yellow Sea and one of China's oldest modern wine regions, centred on Yantai and Penglai, where Changyu was founded in 1892.
climate: Monsoonal maritime: humid with summer rain, which brings disease pressure.
soils: Sandy loams and granite-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Gernischt (Carmenère), Merlot, Marselan, Chardonnay.

name: Rhone
summary: The Rhône Valley runs from Vienne to Avignon, with the steep, Syrah-dominated Northern Rhône (Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage) and the broader, Grenache-led Southern Rhône (Châteauneuf-du-Pape).
climate: Continental in the north; Mediterranean in the south, shaped by the cold Mistral wind.
soils: Granite and schist slopes in the north; galets roulés (large round stones), limestone, sand and clay in the south.
typical_varietals: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne, Cinsault.
blends: Southern Rhône GSM blends (Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits 13 grapes); Northern Syrah co-fermented with Viognier.

name: Bordeaux
summary: The world's benchmark for blended reds, along the Gironde estuary and Garonne and Dordogne rivers, divided into the Left Bank (Médoc, Graves) and Right Bank (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol).
climate: Temperate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Landes forest; vintage variation is significant.
soils: Gravel over clay on the Left Bank (Cabernet); clay and limestone on the Right Bank (Merlot).
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon.
blends: Left Bank Cabernet–Merlot, Right Bank Merlot–Cabernet Franc, white Sauvignon–Semillon, and botrytised Sauternes.

name: Savoie
summary: Alpine region in eastern France near the Swiss and Italian borders, making crisp, light mountain wines from local grapes.
climate: Cool continental and alpine, moderated by lakes (Bourget, Geneva).
soils: Limestone scree, glacial moraine and molasse.
typical_varietals: Jacquère, Altesse (Roussette), Bergeron (Roussanne), Mondeuse, Gamay.
blends: Mostly varietal; Crémant de Savoie sparkling.

name: Loire Valley
summary: France's longest river runs through a string of diverse regions, from Muscadet near the Atlantic through Anjou and Touraine to Sancerre in the east.
climate: Maritime in the west, becoming more continental eastwards; cool overall.
soils: Granite and schist (Muscadet), tuffeau limestone (Touraine, Saumur), flint and Kimmeridgian marl (Sancerre).
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Melon de Bourgogne, Gamay.
blends: Crémant de Loire; Anjou rosé; mostly varietal still wines.

name: Languedoc-Roussillon
summary: A vast Mediterranean arc from the Rhône delta to the Spanish border, transformed from bulk wine to a source of characterful value and old-vine wines.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean with strong winds (Tramontane, Mistral).
soils: Schist, limestone, gravel terraces and clay; Roussillon has black schist.
typical_varietals: Grenache, Syrah, Carignan, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Picpoul, Grenache Blanc.
blends: GSM-plus-Carignan reds; Vins Doux Naturels such as Banyuls and Maury; Crémant de Limoux.

name: Alsace
summary: Long, narrow strip on the foothills of the Vosges mountains bordering Germany, known for aromatic, often varietally labelled whites.
climate: Sunny and dry continental: the Vosges rain shadow makes it one of France's driest regions.
soils: An extremely varied mosaic of granite, limestone, schist, sandstone, volcanic and marl soils across 51 Grand Crus.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir.
blends: Edelzwicker and Gentil field blends; Crémant d'Alsace; late-harvest Vendanges Tardives.

name: Bourgogne
summary: Burgundy, the spiritual home of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, where wine is classified by climat (vineyard plot), from regional to Premier and Grand Cru.
climate: Cool continental, with frost and hail risks; ripening varies a lot between vintages.
soils: Jurassic limestone and marl on the east-facing Côte d'Or slopes; Kimmeridgian clay in Chablis.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Gamay.
blends: Almost always single-varietal; Crémant de Bourgogne.

name: Champagne
summary: The northernmost major French region, around Reims and Épernay, where traditional-method sparkling wine reached its benchmark form.
climate: Cool and marginal continental with Atlantic influence; still wines are naturally high in acid.
soils: Chalk subsoil (porous, retains water, reflects heat) under thin topsoil; marl and clay in the Aube.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier.
blends: Non-vintage house blends across grapes, villages and years; Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs.

name: Beaujolais
summary: Gamay country south of Burgundy, from fresh Beaujolais Nouveau to structured wines from its ten Crus such as Morgon, Fleurie and Moulin-à-Vent.
climate: Semi-continental with Mediterranean influence from the south.
soils: Pink granite in the northern Crus; clay and limestone in the south.
typical_varietals: Gamay, Chardonnay.
blends: Single-varietal Gamay, often made by carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration.

name: Provence
summary: Sun-soaked south-eastern region between the Rhône and the Riviera, the world's reference for pale, dry rosé.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean with the Mistral wind.
soils: Limestone in the west and crystalline schist and granite in the east.
typical_varietals: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Rolle (Vermentino), Tibouren.

name: Nahe
summary: Small region along the Nahe river between the Mosel and Rheinhessen, producing some of Germany's most expressive Riesling from a mosaic of volcanic and slate soils.
climate: Cool continental, sheltered by the Hunsrück hills; dry and sunny for Germany.
soils: A highly varied mix of volcanic porphyry, slate, quartzite, sandstone and loess.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir.

name: Franconia
summary: Franken, in northern Bavaria along the Main river, famous for dry, earthy Silvaner sold in the squat flagon-shaped Bocksbeutel bottle.
climate: Continental, with cold winters, frost risk and warm, dry summers.
soils: Muschelkalk (shell limestone), Keuper marl and red sandstone.
typical_varietals: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).

name: Mosel
summary: Germany's best-known region, where vines cling to precipitous slate slopes above the winding Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers, producing delicate, low-alcohol Riesling.
climate: Cool and marginal; the river and steep south-facing slopes are crucial for ripening.
soils: Blue and red Devonian slate, which retains heat.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Elbling, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Blanc.
blends: Riesling across Prädikat sweetness levels, from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese.

name: Pfalz
summary: Germany's second-largest region, a warm, sunny extension of Alsace, known for full, dry Riesling and increasingly for Pinot Noir.
climate: One of Germany's warmest and driest, sheltered by the Haardt mountains.
soils: Sandstone, limestone, loess, loam and basalt.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Dornfelder, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Spätburgunder.
blends: Mostly varietal; VDP Grosses Gewächs dry wines.

name: Naoussa
summary: PDO in Macedonia, northern Greece, on the slopes of Mount Vermio, home of age-worthy, structured Xinomavro, often compared to Nebbiolo.
climate: Continental, with cold winters, rainfall and altitude (150–350 m).
soils: Varied clay, sand, limestone and marl.
typical_varietals: Xinomavro.
blends: PDO wines are 100% Xinomavro; regional blends with Merlot or Syrah.

name: Peloponnese
summary: Large peninsula in southern Greece that includes Nemea, home of Agiorgitiko, and Mantinia, known for floral, crisp Moschofilero.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, becoming cooler and continental with altitude in the mountainous interior.
soils: Limestone, clay and schist, with sandy coastal soils.
typical_varietals: Agiorgitiko, Moschofilero, Roditis, Mavrodaphne.
blends: Varietal Nemea reds; sweet Mavrodaphne of Patras fortified.

name: Tuscany
summary: Central Italy's iconic region of rolling hills, home to Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano and the coastal 'Super Tuscans' of Bolgheri.
climate: Mediterranean, warm and dry on the coast; more continental and elevated inland.
soils: Galestro (friable schistous clay) and alberese (limestone) in Chianti; coastal gravels and clays in Bolgheri.
typical_varietals: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Colorino, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Vernaccia, Trebbiano.
blends: Chianti (Sangiovese-led); Super Tuscans (Bordeaux varieties with or without Sangiovese); Vin Santo.

name: Sicily
summary: The Mediterranean's largest island, now a vibrant quality region, from the volcanic slopes of Etna to the hot western plains and Marsala.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean; Etna has cool mountain conditions at up to 1,000 m.
soils: Volcanic sands and ash on Etna; limestone, clay and sand elsewhere.
typical_varietals: Nero d'Avola, Nerello Mascalese, Frappato, Grillo, Carricante, Catarratto.
blends: Cerasuolo di Vittoria (Nero d'Avola–Frappato), Etna Rosso (Nerello Mascalese–Cappuccio), Marsala fortified.

name: Sardinia
summary: Rugged island with Spanish-influenced grapes, celebrated for Cannonau (Grenache) and crisp, saline Vermentino.
climate: Hot, dry and windy Mediterranean (the Mistral).
soils: Granite, schist, sand and limestone.
typical_varietals: Cannonau (Grenache), Vermentino, Carignano, Monica, Bovale.
blends: Mostly varietal; Carignano del Sulcis from old bush vines.

name: Puglia
summary: The heel of Italy's boot, a hot, productive region known for ripe, generous reds.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, moderated by two seas.
soils: Red clay (terra rossa) over limestone.
typical_varietals: Primitivo, Negroamaro, Nero di Troia, Malvasia Nera.

name: Emilia-Romagna
summary: Fertile northern region spanning the Po plain, the gastronomic home of Lambrusco and of Sangiovese di Romagna.
climate: Continental with hot, humid summers and foggy winters.
soils: Alluvial plains, clay and limestone in the Apennine foothills.
typical_varietals: Lambrusco (several types), Sangiovese, Albana, Trebbiano, Pignoletto.

name: Marche
summary: Adriatic-coast region of central Italy, best known for the crisp, almond-tinged white Verdicchio.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, continental inland.
soils: Clay, limestone and sandstone.
typical_varietals: Verdicchio, Montepulciano, Sangiovese, Pecorino, Lacrima.

name: Friuli-Venezia Giulia
summary: North-eastern region on the Slovenian border, celebrated for aromatic and textured whites and as a pioneer of skin-contact orange wine.
climate: Cool to moderate, protected from the north by the Alps and cooled by the Adriatic.
soils: Ponca (layered marl and sandstone) in Collio and Colli Orientali; gravel on the plains.
typical_varietals: Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, Refosco, Schioppettino.
blends: White field blends; amber, skin-contact Ribolla.

name: Piemonte
summary: North-western Italy at the foot of the Alps, home of Barolo and Barbaresco (Nebbiolo) and much-loved everyday Barbera, Dolcetto and Moscato d'Asti.
climate: Continental with cold, foggy autumns (nebbia gave Nebbiolo its name).
soils: Calcareous marl and sandstone in the Langhe.
typical_varietals: Nebbiolo, Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato, Arneis, Cortese.

name: Veneto
summary: North-eastern region including Valpolicella, Soave and Prosecco country.
climate: Continental, moderated by Lake Garda and the Adriatic.
soils: Limestone and volcanic basalt (Soave), marl and morainic soils.
typical_varietals: Corvina, Rondinella, Garganega, Glera, Pinot Grigio.
blends: Amarone and Ripasso (dried-grape Valpolicella blends); Prosecco.

name: Hawke's Bay
summary: New Zealand's oldest and second-largest region on the North Island's east coast, its leading source of Bordeaux-style reds and Syrah, especially from the Gimblett Gravels.
climate: Warm and sunny maritime, sheltered by inland ranges.
soils: Varied: free-draining Gimblett Gravels, alluvial silts, and limestone in the hills.
typical_varietals: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Marlborough
summary: New Zealand's largest region at the top of the South Island, which put the country on the map with intensely aromatic Sauvignon Blanc.
climate: Cool, sunny and dry maritime, with a large diurnal range.
soils: Stony alluvial gravels in the Wairau Valley; heavier clays in the Southern Valleys and Awatere.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling.

name: Central Otago
summary: The world's southernmost wine region, a dramatic, mountainous area producing vibrant, concentrated Pinot Noir.
climate: Semi-continental: hot, dry summers, cold winters, frost risk and very high UV.
soils: Wind-blown loess and gravels over schist.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Chardonnay.

name: Wairarapa
summary: Small North Island region around Martinborough, near Wellington, with a reputation for savoury, structured Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool, windy maritime, with dry autumns.
soils: Free-draining alluvial gravel terraces and loess.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Syrah.

name: Duoro
summary: The Douro Valley in northern Portugal, one of the world's oldest demarcated regions (1756), home of Port and of increasingly acclaimed dry reds, grown on steep terraced slopes.
climate: Hot, dry continental, sheltered from the Atlantic by the Marão mountains.
soils: Schist, which is broken up to make terraces and lets roots go deep.
typical_varietals: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão.
blends: Port, and dry red field blends from old mixed plantings.

name: Douro
summary: One of the world's oldest demarcated regions (1756), home of Port and of increasingly acclaimed dry reds, grown on steep terraced slopes along the Douro river.
climate: Hot, dry continental, sheltered from the Atlantic by the Marão mountains.
soils: Schist, which is broken up to make terraces and lets roots go deep.
typical_varietals: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão.
blends: Port, and dry red field blends from old mixed plantings.

name: Lisboa
summary: Atlantic-facing region north of Lisbon, a source of fresh, good-value whites and reds, including the historic sub-regions of Colares and Bucelas.
climate: Maritime, cool and humid, with strong Atlantic winds.
soils: Clay and limestone, with sand dunes at Colares (where vines survived phylloxera).
typical_varietals: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Ramisco.
blends: Blends of Portuguese and international grapes.

name: Stellenbosch
summary: South Africa's most famous region, east of Cape Town, with mountain slopes and valleys producing the country's finest Cabernet, Bordeaux blends and Pinotage.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooled by False Bay breezes and the 'Cape Doctor' wind.
soils: Decomposed granite on mountain slopes and sandstone-derived soils on valley floors.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage, Chenin Blanc, Syrah, Merlot, Chardonnay.

name: Valdapeñas
summary: Valdepeñas, a DO in the south of La Mancha, Castilla-La Mancha, historically supplying Madrid with soft, affordable Tempranillo (locally Cencibel).
climate: Extreme continental: very hot summers, cold winters, low rainfall.
soils: Red-brown clay over limestone, with a chalky crust.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Cencibel), Airén, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Tempranillo, traditionally softened with white Airén.

name: Valdepeñas
summary: DO in the south of La Mancha, Castilla-La Mancha, historically supplying Madrid with soft, affordable Tempranillo (locally Cencibel).
climate: Extreme continental: very hot summers, cold winters, low rainfall.
soils: Red-brown clay over limestone, with a chalky crust.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Cencibel), Airén, Garnacha, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Tempranillo, traditionally softened with white Airén.

name: Rioja
summary: Spain's most famous red region, along the Ebro river in the north, with three sub-zones (Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, Rioja Oriental) and an ageing classification from Joven to Gran Reserva.
climate: Atlantic-influenced continental in the west, warmer and Mediterranean in the east.
soils: Calcareous clay (Alavesa, Alta), ferrous clay and alluvial soils (Oriental).
typical_varietals: Tempranillo, Garnacha, Graciano, Mazuelo (Carignan), Viura.
blends: Tempranillo-led blends with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo, traditionally aged in American oak.

name: Catalonia
summary: North-eastern Spain, home of Cava (around Penedès), the powerful old-vine reds of Priorat and Montsant, and a lively natural-wine scene.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, more continental and elevated inland.
soils: Llicorella (slate and quartz) in Priorat; limestone and clay in Penedès.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Cariñena (Samsó), Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada, Tempranillo (Ull de Llebre).

name: Manchuela
summary: DO on the high plateau between La Mancha and Valencia, revived by producers working with old-vine Bobal.
climate: Continental with Mediterranean influence: hot days, cool nights and altitude (600–1,000 m).
soils: Limestone and clay.
typical_varietals: Bobal, Tempranillo, Garnacha Tintorera, Macabeo, Moravia Agria.

name: Ribera del Duero
summary: High-plateau region along the Duero river in Castilla y León, producing powerful, structured Tempranillo (Tinto Fino), including the legendary Vega Sicilia.
climate: Extreme continental at 750–1,000 m, with a huge diurnal range.
soils: Limestone, chalk and clay with alluvial gravels.
typical_varietals: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino), Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec.

name: Priorat
summary: One of Spain's two DOCa regions, in Catalonia, making concentrated reds from old vines on steep slate terraces.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, moderated by altitude.
soils: Llicorella: crumbly slate and quartz.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Cariñena, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah.
blends: Garnacha–Cariñena with Bordeaux and Rhône varieties.

name: California
summary: Produces around 80% of US wine, from the prestigious North Coast (Napa, Sonoma) through the Central Coast to the high-volume Central Valley.
climate: Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog along the coast; hot inland.
soils: Hugely varied: volcanic, alluvial fans, marine sediments, granite.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Napa Valley
summary: California's most famous AVA, north of San Francisco, renowned for rich, opulent Cabernet Sauvignon.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooler in the south (Carneros) thanks to San Pablo Bay fog.
soils: Over 30 soil series: volcanic on the mountains, alluvial fans on the valley floor.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Zinfandel.

name: Oregon
summary: Pacific Northwest state whose Willamette Valley is America's leading source of Burgundian-style Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool maritime, with wet winters and dry summers.
soils: Volcanic Jory soils, marine sedimentary Willakenzie soils and wind-blown loess.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay.

name: Mendoza
summary: Argentina's dominant region at the foot of the Andes, the world's home of Malbec, with high-altitude vineyards in the Uco Valley.
climate: Dry, sunny high desert (600–1,500 m) with a large diurnal range; irrigated from Andes snowmelt.
soils: Alluvial sands, gravels and limestone deposits.
typical_varietals: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Torrontés, Chardonnay.

name: Adelaide Plains
summary: Flat, warm region on the plains north of Adelaide around Virginia and Angle Vale, long a source of bulk fruit and now home to a handful of estate producers.
climate: Hot and dry Mediterranean with low rainfall; some relief from gulf breezes.
soils: Red-brown sandy loams over limestone and alluvial clays.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Chardonnay, Colombard.

name: Currency Creek
summary: Small Fleurieu Peninsula region around Goolwa and the mouth of the Murray, neighbouring Langhorne Creek and Southern Fleurieu.
climate: Moderate maritime, cooled by breezes off Lake Alexandrina and the Southern Ocean.
soils: Sandy loams and deep sands over clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Merlot.

name: Mount Benson
summary: Young coastal region on the Limestone Coast near Kingston SE, planted from the late 1980s, with vineyards just a few kilometres from the sea.
climate: Cool maritime with strong sea breezes and a long, mild ripening season.
soils: Terra rossa and sandy loams over limestone, with good drainage.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Merlot.

name: Mount Gambier
summary: South Australia's coolest region, around the volcanic city of Mount Gambier at the southern tip of the Limestone Coast.
climate: Cool maritime, with high rainfall and a short, marginal ripening season.
soils: Volcanic ash and loams over limestone, from the region's extinct volcanoes.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.

name: Robe
summary: Coastal Limestone Coast region around the fishing town of Robe, between Mount Benson and Coonawarra, dominated by a few large plantings.
climate: Cool maritime with a long, even growing season moderated by the Southern Ocean.
soils: Terra rossa and sands over limestone ridges.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Merlot, Pinot Noir.

name: Southern Flinders Ranges
summary: South Australia's most northerly region, in the foothills of the southern Flinders Ranges around Wirrabara and Laura, near the top of Spencer Gulf.
climate: Warm, with elevation and gulf breezes cooling nights; dry summers.
soils: Red-brown loams and gravels over quartzite and shale.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Riesling.

name: Ballarat
summary: Cool, high region around the gold-rush city of Ballarat in central Victoria, small in size but noted for fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
climate: Cool continental at 400–600 m, with frost risk and a long, slow ripening season.
soils: Quartz-rich gravelly loams, volcanic basalt soils and clays.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Pinot Gris.

name: Bendigo
summary: Historic central Victorian region around the gold-rush city of Bendigo, known for rich, minty Shiraz and Cabernet from small family vineyards.
climate: Warm continental with hot, dry summers and cool nights; low rainfall.
soils: Gravelly quartz and sandy loams over clay, with ironstone in places.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay.

name: Gippsland
summary: Huge, sparsely planted region covering Victoria's south-east, with small producers making characterful Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
climate: Cool and maritime in the south and west, more continental and drier in the east.
soils: Varied: sandy loams, alluvial river flats, red volcanic and grey clay soils.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Glenrowan
summary: North-east Victorian region near Rutherglen, famous (with it) for fortified Muscat and Topaque, and for robust Durif and Shiraz.
climate: Hot continental with warm days, cool nights and late autumn sugar concentration.
soils: Deep red granitic loams on the slopes of the Warby Ranges.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Durif, Cabernet Sauvignon, Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge, Muscadelle.

name: Henty
summary: Victoria's coolest mainland region, in the far south-west around Drumborg and Portland, known for steely Riesling and sparkling base wine.
climate: Very cool maritime, with long ripening and frost and rain risk.
soils: Volcanic basalt soils, red clays and limestone in the west.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Shiraz.
blends: Traditional-method sparkling; dry and off-dry Riesling.

name: Strathbogie Ranges
summary: Elevated granite plateau in central Victoria between the Goulburn Valley and Upper Goulburn, producing elegant cool-climate wines.
climate: Cool to moderate with altitude (up to 600 m), cool nights and good rainfall.
soils: Decomposed granite sands and loams.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Chardonnay, Shiraz, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Sunbury
summary: Small historic region just north-west of Melbourne, with nineteenth-century wineries such as Craiglee and Goona Warra, known for peppery Shiraz.
climate: Cool and windy, with low rainfall and a long growing season.
soils: Volcanic basalt clays and sandy loams over sandstone.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Swan Hill
summary: Irrigated Murray River region straddling the Victoria–New South Wales border, a large source of everyday and alternative-variety wines.
climate: Hot, dry continental with very low rainfall; irrigation from the Murray.
soils: Red sandy loams and calcareous Mallee soils.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Colombard, Fiano, Nero d'Avola.

name: Upper Goulburn
summary: Mountainous region around Mansfield and Lake Eildon, at the foot of Victoria's Alps, with vineyards from valley floors to high slopes.
climate: Cool to moderate, with altitude moderating warm summers; snow on higher ground.
soils: Granitic and volcanic loams, with alluvial river soils.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Shiraz.

name: Cowra
summary: Central-west New South Wales region on the Lachlan River, which made its name with rich, early-ripening Chardonnay in the 1970s.
climate: Warm continental with hot days and cool nights.
soils: Red-brown loams and granitic sands over clay.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Verdelho.

name: Gundagai
summary: Small southern New South Wales region on the Murrumbidgee River between Hilltops and Tumbarumba.
climate: Warm to moderate continental, with cooler higher sites to the east.
soils: Red-brown loams and granite-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay.

name: Hastings River
summary: Subtropical coastal region around Port Macquarie on the New South Wales mid-north coast, one of Australia's wettest wine regions.
climate: Warm and humid subtropical with summer rainfall, demanding disease-resistant varieties.
soils: Red and brown volcanic loams and alluvial river soils.
typical_varietals: Chambourcin, Chardonnay, Semillon, Verdelho, Shiraz.

name: Hilltops
summary: Elevated region around Young in southern New South Wales, known for structured Shiraz and Cabernet and a growing range of Italian varieties.
climate: Continental at 450–600 m, with warm days, cold nights and frost risk.
soils: Deep red granitic and basalt-derived clay loams.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Nebbiolo, Barbera, Chardonnay.

name: New England Australia
summary: Australia's highest wine region, on the Northern Tablelands of New South Wales around Armidale and Tenterfield.
climate: Cool, high-altitude (up to 1,300 m) with summer rainfall and big diurnal swings.
soils: Granite and basalt-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Shiraz, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Perricoota
summary: Irrigated Murray River region around Moama in southern New South Wales, opposite Echuca.
climate: Hot and dry continental, irrigated from the Murray.
soils: Red sandy loams and river alluvium.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot.

name: Riverina
summary: Large irrigated region around Griffith, one of Australia's biggest producers of everyday wine and home of world-class botrytis Semillon.
climate: Hot, dry continental; humid autumns favour noble rot.
soils: Red-brown loams and grey clays, irrigated from the Murrumbidgee.
typical_varietals: Semillon, Shiraz, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Durif.
blends: Botrytised (noble rot) sweet Semillon; commercial blends.

name: Shoalhaven Coast
summary: Coastal region south of Sydney around Nowra and Berry, with small vineyards supplying cellar doors and tourism.
climate: Warm, humid maritime with summer rainfall.
soils: Volcanic and sandstone-derived loams and river alluvium.
typical_varietals: Chambourcin, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Shiraz, Semillon.

name: Southern Highlands
summary: Elevated region south-west of Sydney around Bowral and Moss Vale, with cool-climate whites and Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool and fairly wet, with altitude of 500–900 m.
soils: Basalt-derived red loams and sandstone soils.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.

name: Tumbarumba
summary: High, cool region on the western slopes of the Snowy Mountains, prized as a source of fine Chardonnay and sparkling base.
climate: Cool alpine (300–800 m), with a short season and frost risk.
soils: Granitic and basalt-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Meunier.

name: Blackwood Valley
summary: Western Australian region around Boyup Brook and Bridgetown, between Margaret River and Great Southern.
climate: Mediterranean, warmer and drier than the coast, with cool nights.
soils: Gravelly loams over clay, and lateritic soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot.

name: Geographe
summary: Coastal region around Bunbury and the Ferguson Valley, north of Margaret River, known for Mediterranean varieties and Shiraz.
climate: Warm Mediterranean with sea breezes; cooler in the elevated Ferguson Valley.
soils: Sandy coastal plain soils, alluvium and gravelly loams in the hills.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Sangiovese.

name: Manjimup
summary: Elevated south-west Western Australian region among karri and jarrah forests, also known for truffles.
climate: Moderate to cool with more continental influence than nearby Pemberton.
soils: Gravelly loams and karri loams over granite.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc.

name: Peel
summary: Region south of Perth around Mandurah, where Peel Estate made a long-lived Shiraz and Chenin Blanc.
climate: Warm to hot Mediterranean with afternoon sea breezes.
soils: Coastal sands, and gravelly loams in the Darling Range foothills.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Pemberton
summary: Cool south-west Western Australian region in the tall karri forests, known for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and crisp Sauvignon Blanc.
climate: Cool and wet maritime, with a long, mild ripening season.
soils: Fertile karri loams and gravelly soils over granite.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Shiraz.

name: Perth Hills
summary: Small-scale region in the Darling Range escarpment just east of Perth, with many boutique wineries.
climate: Warm Mediterranean, cooler than the Swan Valley thanks to altitude.
soils: Gravelly loams and granite-derived soils.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Merlot.

name: Swan District
summary: Western Australia's oldest wine area, including the Swan Valley just north-east of Perth, settled in the 1830s and known for fortified Verdelho and Chenin Blanc.
climate: Hot Mediterranean, one of Australia's hottest regions, with the 'Fremantle Doctor' sea breeze.
soils: Deep alluvial loams and sands.
typical_varietals: Chenin Blanc, Verdelho, Shiraz, Grenache, Chardonnay.

name: Granite Belt
summary: Queensland's leading region, on a high granite plateau around Stanthorpe near the New South Wales border, championing 'Strange Bird' alternative varieties.
climate: Cool for its latitude thanks to altitude (750–1,000 m), with summer rain and frost risk.
soils: Decomposed granite sands, free-draining and low in fertility.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Tempranillo, Fiano, Saperavi.

name: South Burnett
summary: Queensland region around Kingaroy, inland from the Sunshine Coast, with small cellar-door wineries.
climate: Warm subtropical with summer rainfall, moderated by altitude (about 450 m).
soils: Red basalt-derived volcanic soils and sandy loams.
typical_varietals: Shiraz, Chardonnay, Verdelho, Semillon, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Chablis
summary: Burgundy's northernmost district, an outpost in the Yonne making taut, mineral, usually unoaked Chardonnay, graded from Petit Chablis to seven Grand Cru climats.
climate: Cool continental with harsh winters and dangerous spring frosts.
soils: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone full of fossilised oyster shells; Portlandian limestone for Petit Chablis.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay.

name: Côte de Nuits
summary: The northern half of Burgundy's Côte d'Or, from Marsannay to Nuits-Saint-Georges, home to most of the region's red Grand Crus (Chambertin, Musigny, Romanée-Conti).
climate: Cool continental; east-facing slopes catch the morning sun.
soils: Jurassic limestone and marl, with the best sites on mid-slope.
typical_varietals: Pinot Noir, with a little Chardonnay.
blends: Single-varietal Pinot Noir, classified by village, Premier and Grand Cru.

name: Côte de Beaune
summary: The southern half of the Côte d'Or, around Beaune, Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, home of the world's most famous white Burgundy and fine reds from Volnay and Pommard.
climate: Cool continental, slightly warmer and more open than the Côte de Nuits.
soils: Limestone and marl; marlier soils for whites, more iron-rich clay for reds.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.
blends: Single-varietal wines classified by village, Premier and Grand Cru.

name: Mâconnais
summary: Southern Burgundy district between the Côte Chalonnaise and Beaujolais, making ripe, approachable Chardonnay, led by Pouilly-Fuissé.
climate: Moderate continental with Mediterranean hints; warmer than the Côte d'Or.
soils: Limestone and clay, with dramatic limestone outcrops at Solutré and Vergisson.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Gamay, Pinot Noir.

name: Médoc
summary: Bordeaux's Left Bank peninsula north of the city, home to Pauillac, Margaux, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe and most of the 1855-classified châteaux.
climate: Temperate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary; vintage variation is marked.
soils: Deep, warm gravel croupes over clay and limestone, ideal for Cabernet.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot.

name: Graves
summary: The Left Bank south of Bordeaux city, named for its gravels and including Pessac-Léognan (Haut-Brion), producing reds and dry whites.
climate: Temperate maritime, a little warmer than the Médoc.
soils: Gravel and sand over clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon.
blends: Red Bordeaux blends; dry white Sauvignon Blanc–Sémillon.

name: Sauternes
summary: Bordeaux enclave on the Ciron river, with neighbouring Barsac, making the world's most famous botrytised sweet wines, led by Château d'Yquem.
climate: Maritime; autumn mists from the cold Ciron meeting the warm Garonne encourage noble rot.
soils: Gravel, sand and clay over limestone.
typical_varietals: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle.

name: Saint-Émilion
summary: Right Bank Bordeaux appellation around a medieval hilltop town, a UNESCO World Heritage site with its own regularly revised classification.
climate: Maritime with more continental influence than the Left Bank.
soils: Limestone plateau and côtes, clay-limestone slopes and sand and gravel near Pomerol.
typical_varietals: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Pomerol
summary: Tiny, unclassified Right Bank plateau next to Saint-Émilion, home of Pétrus and Le Pin and some of the world's most expensive Merlot.
climate: Maritime with continental influence.
soils: Clay and gravel, with the famous iron-rich blue clay (crasse de fer) at the plateau's heart.
typical_varietals: Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

name: Côte-Rôtie
summary: Steep, terraced northern Rhône appellation above Ampuis, the 'roasted slope', making perfumed Syrah sometimes co-fermented with Viognier.
climate: Continental, with the vines' south-east exposure and steepness capturing heat.
soils: Schist and mica-schist in the Côte Brune; granite and gneiss in the Côte Blonde.
typical_varietals: Syrah, Viognier.
blends: Syrah with up to 20% Viognier, co-fermented.

name: Hermitage
summary: The famous hill above Tain-l'Hermitage in the northern Rhône, making powerful, long-lived Syrah and rich Marsanne–Roussanne whites.
climate: Continental; south-facing hill sheltered from the cold mistral.
soils: Granite in the west, with loess, alluvial stones and clay to the east.
typical_varietals: Syrah, Marsanne, Roussanne.
blends: Syrah (up to 15% white allowed); Marsanne–Roussanne whites; sweet vin de paille.

name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
summary: The southern Rhône's most famous appellation, named for the summer castle of the Avignon popes, allowing thirteen grape varieties.
climate: Hot Mediterranean, swept by the drying mistral wind.
soils: Famous large galets roulés (rounded pudding stones), plus sand, clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne.
blends: Grenache-led blends of up to 13 varieties.

name: Jura
summary: Small, idiosyncratic region in the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland, known for oxidative vin jaune aged under a film of yeast.
climate: Cool continental, with cold winters and wet springs.
soils: Blue, grey and red marls, with limestone.
typical_varietals: Savagnin, Chardonnay, Poulsard (Ploussard), Trousseau, Pinot Noir.
blends: Vin jaune (Savagnin under flor), vin de paille, Crémant du Jura.

name: Southwest France
summary: Scattered collection of appellations between Bordeaux and the Pyrenees, including Cahors, Madiran, Bergerac, Gaillac and Jurançon, with many native grapes.
climate: Maritime in the west becoming warmer and more continental inland.
soils: Varied: limestone plateaux (Cahors), clay and gravel terraces, and Pyrenean foothill soils.
typical_varietals: Malbec (Côt), Tannat, Merlot, Fer Servadou, Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Colombard.
blends: Cahors Malbec; Madiran Tannat; sweet and dry Jurançon.

name: Corsica
summary: Mountainous Mediterranean island with Italian-influenced grapes, best known for Patrimonio and Ajaccio.
climate: Hot Mediterranean, tempered by sea breezes and altitude.
soils: Granite in the south and west, schist and limestone in the north.
typical_varietals: Nielluccio (Sangiovese), Sciaccarellu, Vermentinu, Grenache.

name: Sancerre
summary: Hilltop town and appellation at the eastern end of the Loire, the benchmark for flinty Sauvignon Blanc, facing Pouilly-Fumé across the river.
climate: Cool continental.
soils: Kimmeridgian marl (terres blanches), limestone (caillottes) and flint (silex).
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir.
blends: Single-varietal Sauvignon Blanc; light Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

name: Muscadet
summary: Westernmost Loire region near Nantes and the Atlantic, making crisp, saline whites, often aged on lees (sur lie), classic with oysters.
climate: Maritime, mild and humid.
soils: Gneiss, granite, schist and gabbro.
typical_varietals: Melon de Bourgogne.

name: Bandol
summary: Coastal Provence appellation near Toulon making structured, long-lived Mourvèdre-based reds and serious rosé.
climate: Hot, sunny Mediterranean; terraced amphitheatre facing the sea.
soils: Limestone, sandstone and clay on terraces (restanques).
typical_varietals: Mourvèdre, Grenache, Cinsault.

name: Barolo
summary: Piemonte's most famous DOCG, in the Langhe hills south-west of Alba, making powerful, tannic, long-lived Nebbiolo from mapped crus (MGA).
climate: Continental with cold, foggy autumns; long ripening season.
soils: Tortonian calcareous marl in the west (La Morra, Barolo) and Serravallian sandstone in the east (Serralunga, Monforte).
typical_varietals: Nebbiolo.

name: Barbaresco
summary: Small Langhe DOCG north-east of Alba, Barolo's neighbour, making slightly more approachable and perfumed Nebbiolo.
climate: Continental, a little warmer and closer to the Tanaro than Barolo.
soils: Calcareous marl with sand.
typical_varietals: Nebbiolo.

name: Chianti Classico
summary: The historic heart of Chianti between Florence and Siena, with its black rooster emblem and new village subzones (UGA).
climate: Continental-Mediterranean with altitude (250–600 m) providing cool nights.
soils: Galestro (friable schist), alberese (limestone), sandstone and clay.
typical_varietals: Sangiovese, Canaiolo, Colorino, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon.
blends: Sangiovese-based (at least 80%); Gran Selezione at the top.

name: Montalcino
summary: Hilltop town south of Siena whose Brunello di Montalcino is one of Italy's greatest wines, made from a local Sangiovese clone.
climate: Warmer and drier than Chianti, with Mediterranean influence and protection from Monte Amiata.
soils: Galestro and limestone at height; clay and sand lower down.
typical_varietals: Sangiovese (Brunello).
blends: Brunello di Montalcino and Rosso di Montalcino (100% Sangiovese).

name: Montepulciano
summary: Renaissance hill town in south-east Tuscany making Vino Nobile di Montepulciano from Sangiovese (here called Prugnolo Gentile).
climate: Continental-Mediterranean with warm days and cool nights.
soils: Sand and clay, with marine fossils and tufa.
typical_varietals: Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile), Canaiolo, Mammolo.

name: Bolgheri
summary: Coastal Tuscan zone on the Maremma, birthplace of the 'Super Tuscans' Sassicaia and Ornellaia.
climate: Warm Mediterranean cooled by sea breezes.
soils: Gravel, sand, clay and stony alluvial fans.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Vermentino.

name: Valpolicella
summary: Hills north of Verona making Amarone and Recioto from air-dried grapes, plus lighter Valpolicella and ripasso styles.
climate: Moderate continental, tempered by Lake Garda.
soils: Limestone, marl, volcanic basalt and alluvial gravel.
typical_varietals: Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella, Molinara.

name: Soave
summary: Veneto zone east of Verona making almond-scented whites from Garganega, with the best from the hilly Classico core.
climate: Moderate continental.
soils: Volcanic basalt in the hills, limestone in the west, alluvium on the plain.
typical_varietals: Garganega, Trebbiano di Soave.
blends: Garganega-based dry whites; sweet Recioto di Soave.

name: Prosecco
summary: Sparkling-wine zone across Veneto and Friuli, with the steep hills of Conegliano Valdobbiadene (DOCG) at its heart.
climate: Moderate, with Alpine influence and good rainfall.
soils: Marl, sandstone and moraine in the hills; alluvial plains elsewhere.
typical_varietals: Glera, Verdiso, Bianchetta, Perera, Pinot Noir (rosé).

name: Alto Adige
summary: German-speaking South Tyrol in the Dolomites, Italy's northernmost region, known for crisp, aromatic whites and strong co-operatives.
climate: Alpine-continental with hot, sunny days, cold nights and protection from the Alps.
soils: Porphyry, dolomitic limestone, granite and glacial moraine.
typical_varietals: Pinot Grigio, Pinot Bianco, Gewürztraminer, Sauvignon Blanc, Schiava, Lagrein, Pinot Noir.

name: Trentino
summary: Alpine province around Trento, south of Alto Adige, best known for Trentodoc traditional-method sparkling.
climate: Alpine to sub-Mediterranean around Lake Garda.
soils: Limestone, dolomite, alluvium and moraine.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Teroldego, Marzemino, Nosiola.

name: Franciacorta
summary: Lombardy zone south of Lake Iseo, Italy's leading traditional-method sparkling wine region.
climate: Moderate, tempered by Lake Iseo and the Alps.
soils: Glacial moraine: gravel, sand and limestone.
typical_varietals: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Bianco, Erbamat.

name: Etna
summary: Vineyards on the slopes of Sicily's active volcano, revived since the 2000s, with old bush vines and many pre-phylloxera plantings.
climate: Mountain-Mediterranean (400–1,000 m), with large diurnal shifts and high rainfall for Sicily.
soils: Black volcanic sands and lava stone, varying by contrada.
typical_varietals: Nerello Mascalese, Nerello Cappuccio, Carricante, Catarratto.

name: Campania
summary: Southern region around Naples, home to Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, with grapes dating from Roman times.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast; cooler and continental in the Irpinia hills.
soils: Volcanic ash and tuff (Vesuvius), clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Aglianico, Fiano, Greco, Falanghina, Piedirosso.

name: Abruzzo
summary: Region between the Apennines and the Adriatic, known for generous Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and Cerasuolo rosé.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, continental in the mountains.
soils: Clay and limestone with alluvial soils.
typical_varietals: Montepulciano, Trebbiano d'Abruzzo, Pecorino, Passerina.

name: Basilicata
summary: Small southern region best known for Aglianico del Vulture, grown on the slopes of an extinct volcano.
climate: Continental at altitude (Vulture at 200–700 m), with cool nights.
soils: Volcanic tuff and ash.
typical_varietals: Aglianico, Malvasia, Moscato.

name: Umbria
summary: Landlocked central region best known for tannic Sagrantino di Montefalco and white Orvieto.
climate: Continental with hot summers and cold winters.
soils: Clay, limestone, and volcanic tuff around Orvieto.
typical_varietals: Sagrantino, Sangiovese, Grechetto, Trebbiano.

name: Lombardy
summary: Northern region around Milan, with Valtellina's terraced Alpine Nebbiolo and Oltrepò Pavese as well as Franciacorta.
climate: Continental, Alpine in the north; lakes moderate some areas.
soils: Alpine granite and schist (Valtellina), moraine, limestone and clay.
typical_varietals: Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca), Croatina, Barbera, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
blends: Sforzato di Valtellina (dried-grape Nebbiolo); Oltrepò blends.

name: Valle d'Aosta
summary: Italy's smallest wine region, on steep Alpine terraces along the Dora Baltea, with rare native grapes.
climate: Alpine continental, dry and sunny, with vines up to 1,200 m.
soils: Glacial moraine, sand and granite.
typical_varietals: Petit Rouge, Fumin, Cornalin, Prié Blanc, Petite Arvine, Nebbiolo.

name: Rías Baixas
summary: Atlantic Galician DO of fjord-like estuaries near the Portuguese border, Spain's home of fresh, saline Albariño.
climate: Cool, wet maritime ('green Spain'); vines often trained on pergolas.
soils: Granite-based sandy soils.
typical_varietals: Albariño, Loureiro, Treixadura, Caíño.

name: Ribeira Sacra
summary: Inland Galician DO with dramatic Roman-terraced slopes above the Miño and Sil rivers.
climate: Atlantic with continental influence; hot sunny slopes, cool nights.
soils: Slate and granite.
typical_varietals: Mencía, Godello, Garnacha Tintorera, Merenzao.

name: Bierzo
summary: Mountain basin in north-west Castilla y León on the Camino de Santiago, revived for its old-vine Mencía.
climate: Transitional between Atlantic Galicia and continental Castilla.
soils: Slate and quartz on slopes; clay on valley floors.
typical_varietals: Mencía, Godello, Doña Blanca.

name: Rueda
summary: High-plateau DO in Castilla y León south of Valladolid, Spain's best-known white region for crisp Verdejo.
climate: Extreme continental at 700–850 m, with hot days and cold nights.
soils: Stony alluvial gravels, sand and limestone.
typical_varietals: Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Viura.

name: Toro
summary: Duero valley DO near Zamora making powerful, dark reds from Tinta de Toro (a local Tempranillo).
climate: Extreme continental, hot dry summers and cold winters.
soils: Sandy and clay soils with stones; phylloxera-resistant sands host ungrafted vines.
typical_varietals: Tinta de Toro (Tempranillo), Garnacha, Malvasía, Verdejo.

name: Jerez
summary: The sherry triangle of Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda in Andalucía, ageing fortified wine in solera systems.
climate: Hot Mediterranean with Atlantic influence; humid poniente and dry levante winds.
soils: Bright white albariza chalk that stores winter rain, plus barro clay and arena sand.
typical_varietals: Palomino Fino, Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel.
blends: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado, PX.

name: Penedès
summary: Catalan region south-west of Barcelona, the heartland of Cava and of the Corpinnat and Clàssic Penedès sparkling movements.
climate: Mediterranean, from warm coast to cooler upper Penedès.
soils: Limestone, clay and sandy soils.
typical_varietals: Xarel·lo, Macabeo, Parellada, Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Garnacha.

name: Navarra
summary: Northern region around Pamplona, once known mainly for rosado, now producing varied reds and whites.
climate: Atlantic-influenced in the north, Mediterranean and continental in the south.
soils: Limestone, clay and gravel.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay.

name: Campo de Borja
summary: Aragón DO, styled 'the empire of Garnacha', with old bush vines on the slopes of the Moncayo.
climate: Continental with dry, cold cierzo winds.
soils: Stony limestone and clay.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Tempranillo, Macabeo.

name: Jumilla
summary: South-eastern DO in Murcia, home of rich, ripe Monastrell from old ungrafted vines.
climate: Hot, dry continental-Mediterranean.
soils: Limestone and sandy soils, which kept phylloxera at bay for a long time.
typical_varietals: Monastrell, Garnacha Tintorera, Syrah.

name: Canary Islands
summary: Volcanic Atlantic islands off Africa, with ancient, phylloxera-free vines, including Lanzarote's vines in ash-pit craters (hoyos).
climate: Subtropical, moderated by trade winds and altitude.
soils: Black volcanic ash (picón) and basalt.
typical_varietals: Listán Negro, Listán Blanco, Malvasía, Negramoll, Marmajuelo.

name: Montsant
summary: Catalan DO wrapped around Priorat, making similar, more affordable Garnacha–Cariñena reds.
climate: Mediterranean with continental influence.
soils: Limestone, granite and clay, with some licorella slate.
typical_varietals: Garnacha, Cariñena, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon.

name: Getariako Txakolina
summary: Basque coastal DO near San Sebastián making light, spritzy, high-acid Txakoli, poured from a height.
climate: Cool, wet Atlantic.
soils: Clay and sandstone.
typical_varietals: Hondarrabi Zuri, Hondarrabi Beltza.

name: Vinho Verde
summary: North-west Portugal's large, green Minho region, known for light, fresh and often slightly spritzy whites and fine Alvarinho.
climate: Cool, wet Atlantic.
soils: Granite.
typical_varietals: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto, Avesso, Vinhão.
blends: Light white blends; Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço.

name: Dão
summary: Granite plateau ringed by mountains in central Portugal, making elegant reds and textured Encruzado whites.
climate: Continental, protected from Atlantic and Spanish extremes by mountains.
soils: Sandy granite, with some schist.
typical_varietals: Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro, Jaen, Tinta Roriz, Encruzado.

name: Bairrada
summary: Atlantic region near Coimbra, known for tannic, age-worthy Baga and traditional-method sparkling.
climate: Maritime, mild and wet.
soils: Clay-limestone and sand.
typical_varietals: Baga, Maria Gomes (Fernão Pires), Bical, Arinto.

name: Alentejo
summary: Vast, hot southern plain known for cork forests, ripe, approachable reds and revived amphora (talha) wines.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean-continental.
soils: Schist, granite, limestone and clay.
typical_varietals: Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, Antão Vaz, Arinto.

name: Madeira
summary: Atlantic island making uniquely long-lived fortified wines, deliberately heated and oxidised during ageing.
climate: Subtropical oceanic, humid.
soils: Volcanic basalt on steep terraces (poios).
typical_varietals: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia, Tinta Negra.
blends: Fortified Madeira, from dry Sercial to rich Malmsey.

name: Setúbal
summary: Peninsula south of Lisbon famous for fortified Moscatel de Setúbal.
climate: Warm Mediterranean with Atlantic influence.
soils: Limestone in the Arrábida hills; sand on the plains.
typical_varietals: Moscatel de Setúbal, Castelão, Moscatel Roxo.

name: Tejo
summary: Region along the Tagus river north-east of Lisbon, a source of good-value reds and whites.
climate: Mediterranean with Atlantic influence.
soils: Alluvial river plains, clay-limestone and sand.
typical_varietals: Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Fernão Pires, Arinto.

name: Azores
summary: Mid-Atlantic volcanic islands; Pico's vineyards, in walled basalt plots (currais), are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
climate: Oceanic, mild, humid and windy.
soils: Black basalt lava.
typical_varietals: Arinto dos Açores, Verdelho, Terrantez do Pico.
blends: Saline volcanic whites; traditional fortified Verdelho.

name: Rheingau
summary: South-facing slope along the Rhine between Wiesbaden and Lorch, historically Germany's most aristocratic Riesling region (Schloss Johannisberg, Kloster Eberbach).
climate: Cool continental, with the Rhine reflecting warmth and the Taunus hills sheltering from north winds.
soils: Loess and loam near the river, slate and quartzite higher up.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).
blends: Dry (trocken) to noble-sweet Riesling; Assmannshausen Pinot Noir.

name: Rheinhessen
summary: Germany's largest wine region, in rolling hills west of the Rhine around Mainz and Worms, transformed by a young generation of growers.
climate: Mild and dry, sheltered by surrounding hills.
soils: Loess and limestone, with red slate (Roter Hang) at Nierstein.
typical_varietals: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Dornfelder, Spätburgunder.

name: Baden
summary: Germany's warmest and most southerly region, stretching from Heidelberg to Lake Constance opposite Alsace, a stronghold of the Pinot family.
climate: Warm for Germany, sunny, sheltered by the Black Forest.
soils: Volcanic Kaiserstuhl, loess, limestone and granite.
typical_varietals: Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weissburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Riesling.
blends: Dry Pinot Noir and Pinot Blanc/Gris.

name: Ahr
summary: Tiny, steep valley south of Bonn and one of the world's most northerly red-wine regions, famed for Pinot Noir.
climate: Cool, but steep slate slopes trap heat.
soils: Slate and greywacke, with loess on lower ground.
typical_varietals: Spätburgunder, Frühburgunder, Riesling.

name: Württemberg
summary: Region around Stuttgart along the Neckar, Germany's main red-wine area, with much consumed locally.
climate: Continental, warm summers.
soils: Keuper marl, shell limestone (Muschelkalk) and loess.
typical_varietals: Trollinger, Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier), Riesling.

name: Mittelrhein
summary: Romantic, castle-lined Rhine gorge between Bingen and Bonn, a UNESCO site with steep slate Riesling vineyards.
climate: Cool, moderated by the river.
soils: Slate and greywacke.
typical_varietals: Riesling.

name: Wachau
summary: Stunning Danube valley west of Krems with dry-stone terraces, making world-class dry Riesling and Grüner Veltliner graded Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd.
climate: Meeting point of cool Atlantic and warm Pannonian influences; large day–night swings.
soils: Gneiss and granite on the terraces; loess on lower slopes.
typical_varietals: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling.

name: Kamptal
summary: Valley of the Kamp river around Langenlois, north-east of the Wachau, with the famous Heiligenstein Riesling vineyard.
climate: Warm Pannonian days, cool nights from the Waldviertel forest.
soils: Loess, gneiss and the desert sandstone of the Heiligenstein.
typical_varietals: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Zweigelt.

name: Kremstal
summary: Region around the historic town of Krems, between Wachau and Kamptal, making Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.
climate: Pannonian warmth meets cool northern air.
soils: Loess terraces and primary rock (gneiss).
typical_varietals: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling.

name: Weinviertel
summary: Austria's largest region, north of Vienna up to the Czech border, the original home of peppery Grüner Veltliner.
climate: Dry, continental and cool.
soils: Loess, with clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling, Zweigelt.

name: Burgenland
summary: Eastern state around the shallow Lake Neusiedl, Austria's red-wine heart and home of botrytised sweet wines.
climate: Warm Pannonian continental; the lake's mists encourage noble rot.
soils: Gravel, sand, loess, limestone and slate.
typical_varietals: Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt, St Laurent, Welschriesling, Chardonnay.
blends: Blaufränkisch; Ruster Ausbruch and Trockenbeerenauslese sweet wines.

name: Steiermark
summary: Styria, in Austria's hilly south near Slovenia, celebrated for vivid Sauvignon Blanc from steep slopes.
climate: Moist and mild, with warm Illyrian influence and cool nights.
soils: Sand, marl, slate and volcanic soils.
typical_varietals: Sauvignon Blanc, Morillon (Chardonnay), Gelber Muskateller, Blauer Wildbacher.

name: Wien
summary: Vienna, the only capital city with a significant wine-growing area, known for Gemischter Satz field blends and Heurigen taverns.
climate: Pannonian continental.
soils: Limestone, loess and sandy loam.
typical_varietals: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Weissburgunder.

name: Valais
summary: Switzerland's largest wine canton, along the upper Rhône valley, with some of Europe's highest vineyards.
climate: Dry, sunny Alpine valley with warm foehn winds.
soils: Alluvial fans, schist, limestone and glacial moraine.
typical_varietals: Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir, Gamay, Petite Arvine, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge.

name: Vaud
summary: Terraced vineyards above Lake Geneva, including the UNESCO-listed Lavaux, the home of fine Chasselas.
climate: Moderate, with the lake reflecting light and heat.
soils: Limestone, moraine and alluvium.
typical_varietals: Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamay.

name: Tokaj
summary: Historic north-eastern region whose botrytised Tokaji Aszú was 'the wine of kings, king of wines', with one of the world's first vineyard classifications.
climate: Continental; autumn mists from the Bodrog and Tisza rivers bring noble rot.
soils: Volcanic rhyolite, andesite and loess.
typical_varietals: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárga Muskotály, Kövérszőlő.
blends: Tokaji Aszú, Eszencia and Szamorodni; dry Furmint.

name: Eger
summary: Baroque town in northern Hungary famed for Egri Bikavér ('Bull's Blood') red blends.
climate: Cool continental.
soils: Volcanic tuff, rhyolite and clay.
typical_varietals: Kékfrankos (Blaufränkisch), Kadarka, Pinot Noir, Olaszrizling.
blends: Egri Bikavér (Kékfrankos-based); Egri Csillag white blend.

name: Villány
summary: Hungary's warmest region, in the far south near Croatia, known for rich Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux-style reds.
climate: Sub-Mediterranean, warm and sunny.
soils: Limestone, loess and clay.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Portugieser, Kékfrankos.

name: Goriška Brda
summary: Hilly zone on the Italian border, continuing Friuli's Collio, known for skin-contact (orange) wines and Rebula.
climate: Sub-Mediterranean, warmed by the Adriatic and sheltered by the Alps.
soils: Opoka (flysch marl and sandstone).
typical_varietals: Rebula (Ribolla Gialla), Friulano, Pinot Grigio, Merlot.

name: Dalmatia
summary: Croatia's Adriatic coast and islands, including the Pelješac peninsula and Hvar, home of Plavac Mali and Zinfandel's ancestor, Crljenak Kaštelanski.
climate: Hot Mediterranean.
soils: Limestone and karst, with red terra rossa.
typical_varietals: Plavac Mali, Pošip, Grk, Babić, Tribidrag.

name: Istria
summary: Peninsula at the north of the Adriatic shared with Slovenia, known for Malvazija Istarska and Teran.
climate: Mediterranean on the coast, cooler inland.
soils: Red terra rossa, white limestone, and grey flysch.
typical_varietals: Malvazija Istarska, Teran, Muškat Momjanski.

name: Kakheti
summary: Georgia's main wine region in the Alazani valley under the Caucasus, birthplace of qvevri winemaking, which is about 8,000 years old.
climate: Continental, with the Caucasus blocking cold northern air.
soils: Alluvial, calcareous and cinnamonic soils.
typical_varietals: Saperavi, Rkatsiteli, Mtsvane, Kisi.

name: Santorini
summary: Volcanic Cycladic island with ancient, phylloxera-free vines trained in low baskets (kouloura) against the wind.
climate: Hot, dry and windy; vines live on sea mist.
soils: Volcanic pumice and ash (aspa).
typical_varietals: Assyrtiko, Athiri, Aidani, Mavrotragano.

name: Crete
summary: Greece's largest island, with a 4,000-year winemaking history and a revival of native grapes.
climate: Hot Mediterranean, cooled by altitude and the north wind.
soils: Limestone, clay and schist.
typical_varietals: Vidiano, Liatiko, Kotsifali, Mandilaria, Vilana.

name: Bekaa Valley
summary: High valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains, made famous by Château Musar.
climate: Dry, sunny and continental at 900–1,000 m.
soils: Gravel, clay and limestone.
typical_varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Carignan, Syrah, Obaideh, Merwah.

name: Golan Heights
summary: High-altitude volcanic plateau, Israel's top wine area since the 1980s.
climate: Cool for the region, with altitude up to 1,200 m and snow in winter.
soils: Volcanic basalt and tuff.
